Two Circles, Two Points

CoordinatesGraph TheoryUnit Distance Problem
Game: Two dots each have a circle round them, one step wide. Make the circles cross in as many places as you can.
How to play: Drag the two dots. Every place the circles cross is a spot that is exactly one step from both dots. With the keyboard, press Space to switch dots and use the arrow keys to move.

Look for the math

If two points are both exactly 1 from a third, the third is on both unit circles. Two different circles of the same radius cross in at most two places, so you will never see three. This tiny fact gives the first upper bound for the unit distance problem.

Counting cherries

Among n points with e unit pairs, call a point together with two of its unit neighbours a cherry. A point with d neighbours is the top of d(d−1)/2 cherries. Each pair of points can be the two ends of at most 2 cherries (the page above shows why), so the total is at most 2 · n(n−1)/2 = n(n−1).

Convexity does the rest

The total of d(d−1)/2 over all points is smallest when the degrees are equal, at 2e/n each. That gives (2e/n)(2e/n − 1) ≤ 2(n−1), so

e ≤ n (1 + √(8n − 7)) / 4, about n3/2 / √2.

The test checks the bound on every small graph with the "at most two" property and shows the known best counts (3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 18 for 3 to 9 points) sit just under it. For 9 points the bound allows 20 and the truth is 18.

Better than n3/2

The best proved upper bound is about n4/3, from the crossing number inequality: draw the unit circles' arcs as a graph in the plane and count its crossings in two ways. The cherries here are the same idea in its simplest form.

Slide the number of points up. How close does the bound come to n1.5, and how far is that from the n4/3 that is known to hold?

An original game for coolmaths, after a problem posed by Paul Erdős in 1946 (Wikipedia)
